meaning: Placed after a verb or similar phrase, it turns the whole phrase into a noun meaning “the act of doing ...” (as subject, object, or explanation); at the end of a sentence it is used in rules and notices to give an instruction or prohibition that must be followed.
connection: Verb dictionary form / た form / ない form + こと; sentence-final rule: verb dictionary form / ない form + こと.

senses.label: As the subject
senses.meaning: Turns an action into a noun that comes before 「は」 or 「が」 as the subject. A common pattern is 「〜ことは + adjective」, like “Doing ~ is …” in English.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + ことは／ことが + 難しい・楽しい・大切だ, etc.
examples: Learning a foreign language is difficult.
Exercising every day is important.
Talking with friends is fun.

senses.label: As the object
senses.meaning: The noun phrase becomes the object of words like 「好き」, 「嫌い」, 「得意」 and 「忘れる」. Use it to talk about likes, skills, or things you forgot to do.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + ことが好きだ／ことが得意だ／ことを忘れる
examples: I like cooking.
I forgot to lock the door.
My younger sister is good at singing.

senses.label: In the predicate
senses.meaning: 「AはBことです」 explains a hobby, dream, job and so on. This sentence-final 「こと」 cannot be replaced with 「の」.
senses.connection: Noun は + verb dictionary form + ことです (趣味・夢・仕事, etc.)
examples: My hobby is taking photos.
My dream is to travel around the world.

senses.label: Must ... (instruction)
senses.meaning: Used in written rules, notices, and assignment instructions to tell the reader to do something. Short, commanding, and neutral in tone.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + こと。(e.g. 「提出すること」, 「記入すること」)
examples: Reports must be submitted by Friday.
Names must be written in ballpoint pen.

senses.label: Do not ...
senses.meaning: 「〜ないこと」 expresses a prohibition. Common on signs, in school rules, and in exam instructions.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + こと。(e.g. 「走らないこと」)
examples: No running in the hallways.
Dictionaries may not be used during the exam.

notes: With perception verbs such as 「見る」, 「聞く」, 「見える」 and 「聞こえる」, the object can only take 「の」: ✕「彼が歌うことを聞いた」 → ○「彼が歌うのを聞いた」.
When a sentence ends by explaining “X is ~”, only 「こと」 works: ✕「趣味は本を読むのです」 → ○「趣味は本を読むことです」. With 「のです」 the sentence turns into an explanation, like “(Actually,) I'm reading a book.”
Used only in written rules, notices and assignment instructions. Said aloud to a coworker or customer, 「明日までに提出すること」 sounds like giving orders and is impolite; in speech say 「明日までに提出してください」.
「〜ないこと」 is a prohibition. When reading notices, don't take it as “not having ...”: 「試験中は話さないこと」 means “talking is prohibited during the exam”.
Distinguish it from the nominalizing 「こと」: in 「趣味は走ることだ」, 「こと」 just means “the act of ...”. This usage applies only when the sentence ends on 「こと」 by itself to express a requirement.

etymology: 「こと」 is written 「事」 in kanji and originally means “a matter, an event.” As a formal noun it loses its concrete meaning and merely turns the preceding clause into a noun, so it is usually written in kana. At the end of a sentence it comes from dropping what follows, such as 「〜ことになっている」 or 「〜ことを求める」, and so becomes a written instruction or rule.
formation: 「こと」 is originally the noun “matter, thing.” Put a verb dictionary form etc. before it as a modifier and you get “the thing of doing ...”, so the whole phrase becomes one noun; it can then take 「が」「を」「は」 as subject or object, or 「です」 as a predicate (「趣味は〜ことです」). Because 「こと」 refers to an abstract “matter”, it leans toward abstract actions, habits, and rules, unlike 「の」, which points to a concrete action happening in front of you. By the same logic, rules list each requirement as “the matter of ...” and end the sentence at 「こと」, giving a concise, objective instruction: 「〜こと」 is something to be done, while 「〜ないこと」 lists “not doing” as an item, that is, a prohibition.

similar.title: 〜ということ (nominalizer)
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「という」 is added before 「こと」 to turn the content of a whole statement into a noun, often to pass on information: 「明日休みだということを聞いた」. A verb + 「こと」 refers only to the action itself.

similar.title: 〜てください
similar.explanation: 「てください」 is a polite spoken request. Sentence-final 「こと」 is a written rule and carries no politeness.

similar.title: 〜なさい
similar.explanation: 「なさい」 is a spoken command, mostly from parents or teachers to children. 「こと」 appears mostly in written regulations; it is also an instruction from above to below.

similar.title: 〜ことになっている
similar.explanation: Same origin (both are built on the formal noun 「こと」): 「ことになっている」 explains that “this is the rule”, whereas sentence-final 「こと」 hands down the rule itself.

meaning: Shows that someone can do something, either as an ability or because a place, rule or condition allows it. More formal than the potential form.
connection: Verb dictionary form + ことができる

senses.label: Ability
senses.meaning: Someone has the ability to do something: “can ~”. It sounds more formal and written than the potential form (話せる).
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + ことができる／ことができます／ことができない
examples: My older brother can speak Chinese.
I can swim 100 meters.
I can't write kanji yet.

senses.label: Condition / permission
senses.meaning: Something is possible or allowed in a certain place, or under certain rules or conditions. Common in explanations, notices and announcements.
senses.connection: (place で／method で) + verb dictionary form + ことができます
examples: At this library, you can borrow books for two weeks.
You can buy tickets online.
You can't take photos here.

senses.label: Finally managed to
senses.meaning: The past form 「ことができた」 means you finally achieved something, after effort or once conditions were right.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + ことができた／ことができました
examples: I was able to pass the exam.
I finally got to see him.

notes: Use 「が」 before 「できる」, not 「を」: ✕「漢字を書くことをできる」 → ○「漢字を書くことができる」.
Don't add 「ことができる」 to a potential form: ✕「話せることができる」 → ○「話すことができる」 or 「話せる」. It also doesn't go with verbs that aren't under your control, such as 「わかる」 and 「見える」: ✕「わかることができる」.
Don't use 「〜ことができますか」 to ask someone to do something: 「窓を開けることができますか」 only asks whether they are able to. To make a request, say 「窓を開けてもらえますか」 or 「開けていただけますか」.
Asking a boss or an elder directly about their abilities (「先生は英語を話すことができますか」) sounds like you are testing them, which is rather rude. Ask about habits instead, or use honorifics: 「英語をお話しになりますか」.

etymology: 「できる」 is written 「出来る」 in kanji and originally meant “to appear, to come about, to be completed”. From “a thing can get done” it came to mean “can”. 「こと」 turns the action before it into a noun that acts as the subject of 「できる」.
formation: It has three parts: verb dictionary form + 「こと」, then 「が」, then 「できる」. 「こと」 turns the action into a noun, “the act of doing ~”; 「が」 marks it as the object of 「できる」; and 「できる」 (「出来る」) originally meant “to come about, to be accomplished”. Put together: “the act of doing ~ can be accomplished”, that is, “can do ~”. Because it treats the action as a “matter” and judges objectively whether it can happen, it sounds more formal than the potential form, and it fits statements about what is or isn't possible under rules or conditions: 「ここでたばこを吸うことはできません」.

similar.title: 〜られる・〜える (potential form)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「話せる」 and 「食べられる」 mean the same as 「話すことができる」 and 「食べることができる」. The potential form is shorter and common in conversation; 「ことができる」 is more formal and appears in writing, rules and formal situations.

similar.title: 〜がわかる・〜ができる
similar.explanation: Same origin: the same 「できる」 attached directly to a noun, as in 「料理ができる」 or 「テニスができる」. For a specific action, use a verb + 「ことができる」: 「中華料理を作ることができる」.

similar.title: 〜こと (nominalizer)
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「こと」 on its own only turns an action into a noun; 「ことができる」 builds on it by adding 「が」 + 「できる」 to make an ability pattern.

meaning: Shows the purpose of movement: go / come / return (somewhere) to do something.
connection: Verb masu-stem / action noun + に + 行く・来る・帰る

senses.label: Verb + に行く
senses.meaning: Drop 「ます」 from the verb and add 「に行く」: “go to do ~”. The destination comes first with 「へ／に」, as in 「デパートへ買いに行く」.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem (without ます) + に行く／に来る／に帰る
examples: I'm going to the bookstore in front of the station to buy a magazine.
My friend is coming over to my house this weekend.
At noon, I go home to eat lunch.

senses.label: Noun + に行く
senses.meaning: Nouns that describe an activity (買い物・旅行・散歩, etc.) can take 「に行く」 directly. You can also say 「〜をしに行く」.
senses.connection: Action noun + に行く／に来る (買い物・旅行・散歩・見学, etc.)
examples: I went shopping on Sunday.
I want to go on a trip to Hokkaido during summer vacation.
I'm going out to walk the dog.

notes: For the purpose part, use the masu-stem (the masu-form without 「ます」): ✕「買うに行く」 ✕「買ってに行く」 → ○「買いに行く」.
Only movement verbs such as 「行く・来る・帰る・戻る」 can follow 「に」. If the next verb is not a movement verb, use 「〜ために」: ✕「日本語を勉強しに頑張る」 → ○「日本語を勉強するために頑張る」.
When telling a boss or client that you'll come to see them, use humble language: ✕「明日、会いに行きます」 → ○「明日、ご挨拶に伺います」. A plain 「会いに行きます」 sounds too casual.
「今度遊びに来てください」 and 「今度飲みに行きましょう」 are often just polite phrases in Japan. If no specific date has been set, don't treat them as a real invitation and turn up at someone's door.

etymology: The masu-stem (連用形) of a verb can work as a noun on its own. Add the particle 「に」 for purpose and then a verb of movement, and you get “go / come in order to do ~”.
formation: A verb's masu-stem can work as a noun on its own, like 「買い」 or 「遊び」. It is followed by the case particle 「に」, which marks a direction or goal, and then by 「行く・来る・帰る」. The goal marked by 「に」 here is not a place but “the action you are going to do”, so the whole means “go/come with the goal of doing ~”. Since 「に」 originally marks the destination of movement, only movement verbs can follow it, and the purpose part must be the noun-like masu-stem or an action noun such as 「旅行」 or 「散歩」.

similar.title: 〜ために
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both express purpose. 「ために」 follows the dictionary form, can be followed by any action, and sounds more written: 「留学するためにお金をためる」. 「〜に行く」 can only be followed by movement verbs and is common in speech.

similar.title: 〜てくる
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「買ってくる」 means going to buy something and coming back, focusing on “doing it and returning”; 「買いに行く」 only states the purpose of going, and doesn't say whether you actually bought anything.

similar.title: 〜には (purpose)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「駅に行くには、どう行けばいいですか」 sets out a goal, and the second half gives the way or condition to reach it; 「〜に行く」 describes the act of going “in order to do ~” itself.

meaning: Shows a natural change of state: “become ~”, “get ~”, “turn into ~”.
connection: i-adjective (drop い) + くなる; na-adjective stem / noun + になる

senses.label: i-adjectives
senses.meaning: Change the final 「い」 of an i-adjective to 「く」 and add 「なる」. This shows a quality or state changing naturally. 「いい」 becomes 「よくなる」.
senses.connection: i-adjective (drop い) + くなる (いい → よくなる)
examples: It's October now, and it has gradually gotten colder.
I took some medicine and got better.
Studying Japanese has started to get fun.

senses.label: na-adjectives
senses.meaning: Add 「になる」 to the stem of a na-adjective to show a change into that state.
senses.connection: na-adjective stem + になる (きれい・元気・上手, etc.)
examples: The room got clean.
I practiced every day and got good at the piano.
My illness is cured, and I'm healthy again.

senses.label: Nouns
senses.meaning: Add 「になる」 to a noun to show becoming a certain role, or reaching a time, age or amount.
senses.connection: Noun + になる (job, season, time, age, amount)
examples: I want to become a doctor in the future.
It will soon be spring.
That comes to 3,000 yen in total.

notes: The “become” form of 「いい」 is 「よくなる」: ✕「いくなる」 → ○「よくなる」.
Na-adjectives and nouns take 「になる」, not 「くなる」: ✕「きれいくなる」 → ○「きれいになる」. 「きれい」, 「嫌い」 and 「有名」 look as if they end in 「い」, but they are na-adjectives.
Verbs can't take 「なる」 directly: ✕「泳げるになった」 → ○「泳げるようになった」.

In restaurants and convenience stores you often hear 「こちら、コーヒーになります」, but this is generally regarded as nonstandard “part-timer keigo”. In formal settings, 「コーヒーでございます」 is more appropriate when handing something over.

etymology: 「なる」 is written 「成る」 in kanji and originally meant “to form, to become”. The adjective form 「〜く」 and the particle 「に」 show the result of the change, and 「なる」 shows the change itself.
formation: The i-adjective 「〜く」 form (「寒く」) and the particle 「に」 (「静かに」, 「医者に」) both express “being in a state / as a result”, and 「なる」 (「成る」) originally means “to form, to become”. Together they mean “come to be in a state of ~”: 「く／に」 marks the end point of the change and 「なる」 expresses the change itself. Since the sentence doesn't say who caused the change, it describes natural change; when someone causes it on purpose, 「する」 is used instead. When a cashier says 「全部で三千円になります」, the amount is likewise presented as something that naturally “comes to” 3,000 yen in total.

similar.title: 〜くする・〜にする (making something change)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both express change. 「〜くなる／〜になる」 is natural change, with the thing that changes as the subject; 「〜くする／〜にする」 means someone deliberately makes it change: 「部屋が明るくなった」 vs. 「電気をつけて部屋を明るくした」.

similar.title: 〜ようになる
similar.explanation: Same origin: the same 「なる」 after 「ように」, used with verbs for a change in ability or habit: 「泳げるようになった」. Adjectives and nouns use 「〜くなる／〜になる」 instead.

similar.title: 〜ことになる
similar.explanation: Same origin: the same 「なる」 after 「こと」, meaning something has been decided (not by you) and turned out a certain way: 「来月、大阪へ転勤することになった」.

meaning: Expresses choosing one option from several or deciding something (“I’ll take…”, “let’s make it…”), and also deliberately making something become a certain state (“to make… into…”).
connection: Noun + にする (choice / decision); い-adjective stem + くする; な-adjective stem／noun + にする (making change)
etymology: 「する」 originally means “to do”. 「Xにする」 means “to make it X”, which when used for choices extends to “settle the choice on X”, i.e. “decide on X”. 「〜く」 and 「〜に」 are the continuative (adverbial) forms of adjectives; followed by 「する」 they mean “make it so that it is…”, forming the pair “deliberate change / natural change” with 「なる」.
formation: 「に」 marks the result of a change or outcome, and 「する」 is “do, make”, so 「Xにする」 literally means “make (the matter) X”. Faced with several options, “making the choice X” is “settling on X, choosing X”; since the speaker actively “makes” it so, it shows one’s own choice and decision, whereas 「Xになる」 is “naturally becoming X” and only states the result. If X is the continuative form of an adjective (「〜く」, 「〜に」), “make it into X” means deliberately bringing something into a certain state, with the changed object marked by 「を」; 「静かにしてください」 literally means “please make (yourself) quiet”, so it can also ask others to stay in a certain state. The same 「にする」 therefore expresses either choice and decision or causing change, depending on whether a noun option or an adjectival state comes before it. Only a noun can precede 「に」, so to decide on an action you must first nominalize it with 「こと」, giving 「〜ことにする」.

senses.label: Choosing / ordering
senses.meaning: Picking one of several options. Very common when ordering food or shopping. 「〜にします」 means “I'll take this one”.
senses.connection: Noun + にします／にしよう; questions: 何にしますか／どれにする
examples: I'll have coffee.
Let's go with the A set for lunch.
I still can't decide which one to get.

senses.label: Deciding / settling
senses.meaning: Deciding on a date, place, plan and so on. The past form 「〜にしました」 means it has already been decided.
senses.connection: (time / place / plan) + にする／にしました／にしましょう
examples: Let's make the meeting next Monday.
I decided on a watch for the birthday present.
We picked Okinawa for our trip.

senses.label: Making change (い-adjective)
senses.meaning: Deliberately changing the quality or state of something: “make it ...”, “turn it ...”. It's the counterpart of 「〜くなる」 (a natural change).
senses.connection: い-adjective stem + くする (明るくする・小さくする・短くする)
examples: I made the room brighter.
Please turn the volume down a little.
I want to cut my hair short.

senses.label: Making change (な-adjective)
senses.meaning: Making something a certain way, or asking someone to stay a certain way. 「静かにしてください」 is a very common request.
senses.connection: な-adjective stem + にする (きれいにする・静かにする・大切にする)
examples: Please be quiet in the library.
Let's all clean up the room together.
Please take good care of yourself.

notes: To decide on doing an action, first turn the verb into a noun with 「こと」: ✕「日本へ行くにする」 → ○「日本へ行くことにする」.
When ordering, 「コーヒーでいいです」 suggests “coffee will do, I suppose”, which sounds rude to someone treating you or to your host. Say 「コーヒーにします」 or 「コーヒーがいいです」.

A deliberate change uses 「〜くする」 (object with 「を」); a natural change uses 「〜くなる」 (subject with 「が」). Pick the wrong one and the meaning changes: 「部屋を暖かくした」 (I warmed up the room) vs. 「部屋が暖かくなった」 (the room got warm).
な-adjectives take 「に」, not 「く」: ✕「静かくしてください」→ ○「静かにしてください」. 「きれい」 and 「嫌い」 are な-adjectives too: ✕「きれいくする」→ ○「きれいにする」.
In 「部屋を静かにする」 and 「明るくする」, 「〜にする／〜くする」 means “make something ~”, not a choice. Tell them apart by what comes before: a noun option, or an adjective describing a state.

similar.title: 〜ことにする
similar.explanation: Same origin: here too 「にする」 expresses a decision, but with a verb before it you need 「〜ことにする」: 「タクシーで行くことにした」. 「〜にする」 takes a noun.

similar.title: 〜くなる・〜になる
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both can state the outcome of a decision. 「〜にする」 is your own decision; 「〜になる」 is a natural outcome or one decided by others: 「会議は月曜日にしました」 (we decided) vs. 「会議は月曜日になりました」 (it has been set).

similar.title: 〜をください
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both can be used when ordering. 「コーヒーをください」 asks the staff directly for something; 「コーヒーにします」 states your choice, sounds softer, and also works when deciding together with friends.

similar.title: 〜ようにする
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「にする」 attached to 「〜よう」, meaning making an effort to turn a behavior into a habit: 「毎日野菜を食べるようにしている」. This pattern, by contrast, directly changes the nature or state of something.

meaning: Shows the order of actions: finish A first, then do B. It also means “since ~”.

senses.label: A first, then B
senses.meaning: Stresses that B happens only after A is finished. It highlights the order more than a plain te-form link. Like “after ~” or “once ~”.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + から + next action
examples: Let's wash our hands first, and then eat.
I'll go out to play after I do my homework.
Please think it over carefully before you decide.

senses.label: Since ~
senses.meaning: From A as a starting point up to now. The second half is often 「〜年になる」, 「ずっと〜」 or another phrase showing time passing or a continuing state.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + から + length of time／ずっと〜
examples: It's already been two years since I came to Japan.
I've lived in this town ever since I got married.
Since I met her, every day has been fun.

notes: You must use the te-form: 「食べたから」 means “because I ate” (a reason); only 「食べてから」 means “after eating”. ✕「宿題をしたから遊びに行く」 (= I'm going out to play because I did my homework) → ○「宿題をしてから遊びに行く」.
For “since ~”, only 「〜てから」 works: ✕「日本に来たあとで二年になる」 → ○「日本に来てから二年になる」.

「〜てから」 stresses “finish A first”, so it is often used to make an order clear to the listener: 「確認してからお返事します」. For a simple chain of actions the plain te-form is enough, as in 「起きて、顔を洗って、出かけた」; there's no need to add 「から」 to each step.

daily.title: Parents giving instructions
daily.description: A mother tells her child to finish homework before watching TV.
daily.example: Finish your homework before you watch TV.

daily.title: Promising to call
daily.description: Telling a friend you'll call after work.
daily.example: I'll call you after I get off work.

work.title: Replying to a client
work.description: After a client's inquiry, checking the details before answering.
work.example: We will contact you after checking the details.

work.title: Introducing yourself
work.description: Talking about your work history at a department meeting.
work.example: It's been three years since I joined the company.

etymology: 「から」 is a case particle marking a starting point, as in 「東京から」. After the te-form it means “with this action as the starting point”, which gives the meanings “after ~” and “since ~”.
formation: It is the verb te-form + the case particle 「から」. The te-form shows that one action is completed and leads on to the next; 「から」 is originally a case particle marking a starting point (「東京から」, 「九時から」). “Do A + 「から」” therefore means “taking the completion of A as the starting point”, so the second action always happens only after the first is finished, stressing “first ~, then ~”. Place that starting point on a timeline and the second part can describe a state that has continued, or time that has passed, ever since, which gives the meaning “since ~”. The reason 「から」 attaches to the plain form (「食べたから」) and is a different structure.

similar.title: 〜たあとで
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both mean “after ~”. 「〜たあとで」 only says that B comes after A, possibly much later; 「〜てから」 stresses the order “A first, and only then B”. For “since ~”, only 「〜てから」 works.

similar.title: 〜て (te-form: linking and sequence)
similar.explanation: Same origin: the same te-form. On its own it can link several actions, simply listing them in order; adding 「から」 highlights “finish this first, then do that”.

similar.title: 〜てからでないと
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「でないと」 is added after 「〜てから」 to mean “you can't ~ unless you first ~”: 「確認してからでないと、お答えできません」.

similar.title: 〜てからというもの
similar.explanation: Same origin: a written expression stressing that things changed dramatically “ever since ~”: 「子どもが生まれてからというもの、生活が一変した」. It is stronger than 「〜てから」.

meaning: Shows the time when something happens or a state exists: “when ~”.
connection: Verb plain form / i-adjective / na-adjective + な / noun + の + とき

senses.label: Nouns / adjectives
senses.meaning: Attaches to nouns or adjectives to mean “at a time when ~”, or “during a certain period”. Nouns take 「の」 and na-adjectives take 「な」.
senses.connection: Noun + の / na-adjective + な / i-adjective + とき
examples: When I was a child, I often played in the river.
What do you do when you have free time?
When it's cold, I feel like having a hot soup.

senses.label: Dictionary form + とき
senses.meaning: B happens before action A is completed (or at the same time). The point is “when about to do A, before it is done”.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + とき (A happens after B or at the same time)
examples: When I went to Japan, I bought a book at the airport (before leaving).
Please turn off the light when you go to bed.
When you leave the house, you say 「行ってきます」.

senses.label: ta-form + とき
senses.meaning: B happens after action A is completed. Use the ta-form whether the whole sentence is present or past.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + とき (A is completed first)
examples: When I went to Japan, I met a friend (after arriving).
When you get home, you say 「ただいま」.
When you're in trouble, feel free to talk to me anytime.

notes: Dictionary form or ta-form depends on which of the two actions comes first, and getting it wrong changes the meaning: 「日本へ行くとき、カメラを買った」 = bought it before leaving (at home); 「日本へ行ったとき、カメラを買った」 = bought it after arriving in Japan.
Nouns need 「の」 and na-adjectives need 「な」: ✕「子どもとき」 ✕「暇とき」 → ○「子どもの時」 「暇なとき」.
Mark the subject of the first clause with 「が」, not 「は」: ✕「母は来たとき、私は寝ていた」 → ○「母が来たとき、私は寝ていた」.
When written in kanji as 「時」, it is still read 「とき」. The 「時」 in 「三時」 is read 「じ」 and means o'clock; that is not this pattern.

daily.title: Childhood memories
daily.description: Chatting with a friend about when you were little.
daily.example: When I was little, I often went to my grandma's house.

daily.title: Comforting a friend
daily.description: A friend has a problem, and you tell them they can come to you anytime.
daily.example: If you're ever in trouble, just tell me.

work.title: Rules for time off
work.description: A manager explains the rules for taking days off.
work.example: When you take a day off, please let us know in advance.

work.title: Customer support
work.description: Contact details written at the end of a manual or an email.
work.example: If you have any questions, please contact us here.

etymology: 「とき」 is written 「時」 in kanji and means “time”. Used as a dependent noun after a clause, it shows when something happens.
formation: 「とき」 (「時」) is originally a noun meaning “time, occasion”. Put a sentence in front of it as a modifier and “the time when ~” becomes a time expression, so it connects just like any ordinary noun: nouns take 「の」, na-adjectives take 「な」, and verbs and i-adjectives use the plain form directly. Because the first part is a modifying clause, its subject takes 「が」. Whether the first part is in the dictionary form or the ta-form shows whether that action is “not yet completed” or “already completed” relative to the second part, not whether the whole sentence is past or future.

similar.title: 〜たら
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜たら」 can also mean “after ~ / when ~”, but it has a conditional nuance and the second half can be a request or intention: 「駅に着いたら電話してください」 is more natural than 「着いたとき電話して」. 「〜とき」 only states the time.

similar.title: 〜場合は
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜場合は」 is used for hypothetical situations, often in rules and manuals, and sounds formal: 「火事の場合は、エレベーターを使わないでください」. 「〜とき」 focuses on actual time.

similar.title: 〜間・〜間に
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both express time. 「〜間」 refers to a continuous stretch of time, “throughout ~”; 「〜とき」 usually refers to a point in time or a certain state: 「夏休みの間、ずっと国にいた」.

meaning: “Do B without doing A”: do B while A has not been done, or do B instead of A.

senses.label: Without doing
senses.meaning: B is done while A has not been done. Often used when A should have been done but wasn't. Like “without ~ing”.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + で + action (食べないで・持たないで, etc.)
examples: This morning I went to school without eating breakfast.
I went out without an umbrella and got wet in the rain.
I read the newspaper without using a dictionary.

senses.label: B instead of A
senses.meaning: Instead of doing A, you do something else, B. The two actions replace each other.
senses.connection: A (verb nai-form) + で、B
examples: Yesterday I didn't study; I played games all day instead.
Instead of taking the bus, I walked to the station.
He didn't go to college; he works at his father's shop.

notes: Don't use 「ないで」 for a reason; use 「なくて」: ✕「お金がないで困った」 → ○「お金がなくて困った」.
Sentence-final 「〜ないで。」 is a casual request, “Don't ~”, and is very rude to a boss or client. Use 「〜ないでください」, or more politely 「〜ないでいただけますか」.
In the written form 「〜ずに」, 「する」 becomes 「せずに」: ✕「連絡しずに休んだ」 → ○「連絡せずに休んだ」.

daily.title: Admitting a slip
daily.description: Telling a friend you were so tired last night that you went straight to bed.
daily.example: I was so tired yesterday that I fell asleep without even taking a shower.

daily.title: A travel story
daily.description: Telling a friend about a trip you took alone without telling anyone.
daily.example: I went on a trip by myself without telling my parents.

work.title: Apologizing to your boss
work.description: Apologizing for sending an email without checking it.
work.example: I'm very sorry for sending it without checking.

work.title: Training goals
work.description: A trainer sets a goal for new employees.
work.example: Please learn to operate it without looking at the manual.

etymology: Formed from the negative 「ない」 plus 「で」, which shows manner or state. The written equivalent 「〜ずに」 comes from the old negative auxiliary 「ず」 plus 「に」.
formation: It is the verb nai-form 「〜ない」 + 「で」. 「ない」 means not doing an action, and 「で」 links like a te-form, attaching “the state of not doing A” to the main action B. So the first part only explains “in what state” B is done, or “instead of what”: 「傘を持たないで出かけた」 = went out without an umbrella; 「バスに乗らないで歩いた」 = walked instead of taking the bus. Because the first part is an accompanying state rather than a reason, for a reason you switch to the other te-form of 「ない」, 「なくて」.

similar.title: 〜ずに
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜ずに」 means the same as 「〜ないで」 but is more written: 「何も言わずに帰った」. 「する」 becomes 「せずに」.

similar.title: 〜なくて (reason)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning, and the easiest to mix up: 「〜なくて」 expresses a reason or links two facts: 「宿題が終わらなくて、寝られなかった」. 「〜ないで」 shows how an action is done or what is done instead, never a reason.

similar.title: 〜ないでください
similar.explanation: Same origin: adding 「ください」 after 「ないで」 turns it into a request not to do something: 「ここでたばこを吸わないでください」. This pattern, by contrast, describes “doing ~ without doing ~”.

meaning: Shows that something is not necessary: “don't have to ~”, “it's OK not to ~”.
connection: Verb nai-form (drop い) + くてもいい

senses.label: No need to do
senses.meaning: Says that something does not need to be done: “you don't have to ~”, “no need to ~”.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form, drop い + くてもいい (行かなくてもいい・来なくてもいい)
examples: You don't have to come tomorrow.
You don't have to eat all of it.
There's no need to hurry.

senses.label: Asking if you can skip something
senses.meaning: 「〜なくてもいいですか」 asks for permission not to do something. Yes: 「はい、〜なくてもいいです」. No: usually 「いいえ、〜なければなりません」.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form, drop い + くてもいいですか
examples: Is it OK if I don't take off my shoes?
Is it OK if I don't hand in this document today?

senses.label: Adjectives / nouns
senses.meaning: Negative forms of adjectives and nouns also work. They relax a condition: “it's fine even if it isn't ~”.
senses.connection: i-adjective + くなくてもいい / noun・na-adjective + じゃなくてもいい
examples: The room doesn't have to be big.
Is it OK if I'm not Japanese?
It's fine if you're not good at it. Just give it a try.

notes: When asked 「〜なくてもいいですか」 and you need to answer “No, you have to”, say 「いいえ、〜なければなりません」: ✕「いいえ、〜なくてもよくないです」.
One small change flips the meaning: 「食べてもいい」 = you may eat; 「食べなくてもいい」 = you don't have to eat.
Saying 「来なくてもいいです」 directly to a guest or your boss may come across as “I don't care whether you come”, which feels cold. 「ご無理なさらなくても大丈夫です」 or 「お忙しければ、いらっしゃらなくても構いません」 is more considerate.
Form it by dropping 「い」 from the nai-form and adding 「くても」: ✕「行かないてもいい」 → ○「行かなくてもいい」.

daily.title: A friend visits
daily.description: The host tells a guest they don't need to take off their shoes.
daily.example: You don't need to take off your shoes.

daily.title: At the convenience store
daily.description: A clerk asks about a bag, and the customer says they don't need one.
daily.example: I'm fine without a bag.

work.title: A considerate boss
work.description: Work has wrapped up, and the boss tells staff to go home early.
work.example: You don't have to work overtime today.

work.title: Paperwork
work.description: A clerk at the counter explains that no personal seal is needed.
work.example: You don't need to stamp your seal.

etymology: Made from 「なくて」 (te-form of the negative 「ない」) + 「も」 (“even”) + 「いい」 (“good, OK”). Literally “even if you don't ~, it's OK”, which shows there is no need.
formation: It is 「なくて」 (the te-form of the negative 「ない」) + 「も」 (even if) + 「いい」 (good, fine): literally “even if you don't, it's fine”. It sets up “not doing it” as a hypothetical condition and then judges that condition as “no problem”, which gives “there is no need to do it”. The same skeleton in the affirmative, 「〜てもいい」, gives permission, “you may do it”; swap 「いい」 for 「かまわない」 or 「大丈夫」 to sound more formal or more considerate.

similar.title: 〜ことはない
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: it also means “there's no need”, but is mostly used to reassure or encourage someone: 「そんなに心配することはないよ」. 「〜なくてもいい」 just states objectively that it's fine not to.

similar.title: 〜てもかまわない
similar.explanation: Same origin: the same 「ても」 + evaluation structure. 「〜なくてもかまわない」 is more formal than 「〜なくてもいい」 and suits clients and bosses.

similar.title: 〜てもいい
similar.explanation: Same origin: the same 「ても」 + 「いい」 structure. With the affirmative form it gives permission, “you may”; only with the negative 「なくても」 does it mean “you don't have to”.

similar.title: 〜ずに済む・〜ないで済む
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: something you would normally have had to do turned out to be unnecessary, with a sense of relief: 「タクシーを使わずに済んだ」. 「〜なくてもいい」 only says it isn't necessary, with no relief.

meaning: Shows obligation or need: “have to ~”, “must ~”. Fairly conversational.
connection: Verb nai-form + と + いけない／だめだ

senses.label: Have to do
senses.meaning: Something must be done because of rules, common sense or your own situation. More conversational than 「〜なければならない」.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + といけない／といけません
examples: I have to get up early tomorrow.
You have to take this medicine every day.
I really have to go home now.

senses.label: A required condition
senses.meaning: Negative forms of adjectives and nouns + 「といけない／とだめだ」 state a condition that must be met.
senses.connection: i-adjective + くないと / noun・na-adjective + じゃないと + いけない・だめだ
examples: Passwords must be at least eight characters long.
You have to be quiet in the library.

senses.label: Dropping the ending
senses.meaning: In speech, 「いけない」 is often dropped, leaving just 「〜ないと」: “I've got to ~”. Common when talking to yourself or telling someone what you need to do.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + と。／ないとね／ないとな
examples: Oh, look at the time. I've got to go.
I have a test tomorrow, so I'd better study.

notes: Don't drop 「ない」: 「行くといけない」 means “it would be bad to go” (discouraging), the exact opposite of 「行かないといけない」 (must go).
Using 「〜ないといけません」 to tell a boss or client to do something sounds forceful, like an order. Usually say 「〜ていただけますか」 or 「〜ていただく必要がございます」.
Cutting it short to 「〜ないと」 is only for speech. In formal emails and documents write it out in full, or use 「〜なければなりません」.

daily.title: Talking to yourself
daily.description: Seeing the pile of dirty clothes, you remind yourself.
daily.example: I'd better do the laundry soon.

daily.title: Leaving early
daily.description: Telling friends you have to leave partway through a party.
daily.example: Sorry, I have to get going.

work.title: A deadline
work.description: Coworkers check a deadline.
work.example: This report has to be submitted by the end of today.

work.title: Coaching a newcomer
work.description: A senior colleague reminds a new employee about polite language.
work.example: You have to use keigo with customers, OK?

etymology: Made from the negative 「ない」 + the conditional particle 「と」 + 「いけない」 (“no good”). Literally “if you don't, it's no good”. 「いけない」 is the negative of 「行ける」 (“can go, works out”), so it means “doesn't work, is bad”.
formation: It is the negative 「ない」 + the conditional particle 「と」 + 「いけない」. 「〜ないと」 means “if you don't”, and 「いけない」 means “won't do, no good”; together, “if you don't, it's no good”, which expresses “must” from the opposite side. Because it is a conditional, “if you don't ~, there will be trouble”, the second half 「いけない」 can be dropped and 「〜ないと」 alone keeps the same meaning. 「いけない」 is originally the negative of 「行ける」 (can go, works out), so at heart it says “carrying on like this won't work”.

similar.title: 〜なければならない
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: basically the same, both mean “must”. 「〜なければならない」 is more formal and common in writing and rules; 「〜ないといけない」 is more conversational and often used about your own specific situation.

similar.title: 〜なくちゃ・〜なきゃ
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: the colloquial contractions of 「〜なくては／〜なければ」. More casual, used only with people you're close to: 「もう行かなきゃ」.

similar.title: 〜ないと (if not)
similar.explanation: Same origin: the same 「〜ないと」 followed by a full result clause becomes a condition, “if you don't ~, then ~”: 「急がないと、遅れるよ」. This pattern simply fixes the result as 「いけない」.

similar.title: 〜てはいけない
similar.explanation: Same origin: it also uses 「いけない」 for “not OK”, but after 「〜ては」 it expresses a prohibition, “must not do”, while after 「〜ないと」 it expresses an obligation, “must do”.

meaning: Offers to do something for the listener, or suggests doing something together while asking the listener's opinion.
connection: Verb masu-stem (drop ます) + ましょうか

senses.label: Offering help
senses.meaning: The speaker offers to do something for the listener: “Shall I ~?”, “Do you want me to ~?”. It leaves the decision to the listener, so it sounds polite.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + ましょうか (the doer is “I”)
examples: Shall I carry your bag?
Shall I open the window?
Shall I take you to the station?

senses.label: Suggesting something together
senses.meaning: Suggests that both people do something together, while asking the listener's opinion: “Shall we ~?”.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + ましょうか (the doer is “we”)
examples: Shall we take a short break?
Shall we get started?

senses.label: Working out details
senses.meaning: Used with question words to discuss times, places, methods and so on.
senses.connection: Question word (何・どこ・いつ, etc.) + verb masu-stem + ましょうか
examples: What time shall we meet?
Where shall we eat?

notes: When offering to help a boss or client, don't say 「〜てあげましょうか」; it sounds as if you're doing them a favor. Use humble forms: 「お持ちしましょうか」, 「お手伝いしましょうか」.
Don't get the direction backwards: 「手伝いましょうか」 means “Shall I help you?”. To ask someone to help you, say 「手伝ってもらえませんか」.
The plain forms 「持とうか」 and 「手伝おうか」 are only for friends and family. With people you've just met or your boss, use 「〜ましょうか」 or a more polite humble form.

daily.title: Helping an older person
daily.description: At the station, you see an older person carrying something heavy and offer to help.
daily.example: May I carry your bags for you?

daily.title: Deciding where to go
daily.description: After a meal, discussing with friends where to go next.
daily.example: Where shall we go next?

work.title: Chairing a meeting
work.description: Everyone has arrived, and the chair announces the start.
work.example: Well then, shall we start the meeting?

work.title: Offering to a client
work.description: On the phone, offering to send materials to a client.
work.example: Shall I send you some detailed materials?

etymology: 「ましょう」 is the volitional / conjectural form of the polite auxiliary 「ます」. It was once written 「ませう」 and expresses intention or invitation. Adding the question particle 「か」 turns it into asking the listener's opinion.
formation: 「ましょう」 is the volitional form of the polite auxiliary 「ます」 (the polite counterpart of 「〜(よ)う」), meaning “I'll do / let's do”, and 「か」 is the question particle. Offering your intention to the other person as a question gives “Shall I ~?” or “Shall we ~?”. When the subject is “I”, it offers help; when it is “we”, it makes a suggestion. Because it asks whether the other person wants it, it is softer than a direct 「〜ましょう」.

similar.title: 〜ましょう
similar.explanation: Same origin: without 「か」 it is a direct suggestion, “let's ~”. 「〜ましょうか」 adds a questioning tone that leaves the decision to the other person, so it is softer and can also offer help.

similar.title: 〜ませんか
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜ませんか」 invites the other person to join, putting their wishes first; 「〜ましょうか」 is mostly a suggestion when both sides already want to do something, or the speaker offering to help.

similar.title: 〜(よ)う (volitional form)
similar.explanation: Same origin: the plain form of 「ましょう」 is the volitional form, so 「持とうか」 and 「行こうか」 are the plain versions of 「〜ましょうか」, used among friends and family.

meaning: A polite guess: “probably ~”, “I suppose ~”. With rising intonation, it checks with the listener: “~, right?”.
connection: Verb / i-adjective plain form / na-adjective stem / noun + でしょう

senses.label: Guessing
senses.meaning: A guess the speaker is not completely sure of. Often paired with 「たぶん」 or 「きっと」. Very common in weather forecasts.
senses.connection: Plain form + でしょう (no 「だ」 after na-adjectives and nouns)
examples: It will probably rain tomorrow.
He probably won't come.
I'm sure the exam will go fine.

senses.label: Confirming (rising tone)
senses.meaning: Said with rising intonation. The speaker thinks the listener also knows or agrees, and checks with them. In speech it often becomes 「でしょ？」.
senses.connection: Plain form + でしょう？／でしょ？
examples: This cake is delicious, isn't it?
See? I told you, didn't I?
You're coming to the party tomorrow, right?

senses.label: Polite questions
senses.meaning: 「〜でしょうか」 is softer and more polite than 「〜ですか」. Use it with shop staff, your boss or strangers.
senses.connection: Plain form / noun + でしょうか
examples: Excuse me, which way is the station?
What time does tomorrow's meeting start?

notes: Don't add 「だ」 after nouns and na-adjectives: ✕「静かだでしょう」 → ○「静かでしょう」.
「〜でしょう？」 with rising intonation implies “You should know that / I told you so”, which is very rude to a boss or client. To check something, say 「〜ですよね」 or 「〜ではないでしょうか」.
When sharing your own guess with a boss, 「〜でしょう」 sounds like you are passing judgment; 「〜と思います」 is safer.
「〜でしょうか」 is a polite question (「駅はどちらでしょうか」), not a guess. Answer with 「〜です」, not 「〜でしょう」.

daily.title: Weather forecast
daily.description: A TV weather forecaster gives tomorrow's weather.
daily.example: Tomorrow will be sunny across most of the country.

daily.title: Showing off to a friend
daily.description: Showing a friend something you just bought and hoping they'll agree.
daily.example: Isn't this pretty? I bought it yesterday.

work.title: Checking with a customer
work.description: A clerk brings some clothes and politely checks with the customer.
work.example: Would this size be all right?

work.title: Scheduling with a client
work.description: Asking a client by email or phone if a time works.
work.example: Would next Wednesday work for you?

etymology: 「でしょう」 can be seen as the conjectural form of 「です」 (old spelling 「でせう」). Its plain counterpart is 「だろう」. The final 「う」 comes from 「む」, an old auxiliary for guesses and intentions.
formation: 「でしょう」 comes from 「でしょ」, the irrealis form of 「です」, + 「う」, the auxiliary of conjecture (historically written 「でせう」). 「です」 is an assertion, “it is ~”; adding the conjectural 「う」 weakens it to “it's probably ~”. Since 「です」 is polite, the whole is a polite guess, the counterpart of the plain 「だろう」. Said with rising intonation, the same guess becomes a bid for agreement, “~, right?”; adding the question particle 「か」 gives 「〜でしょうか」, a soft question that avoids asking too directly.

similar.title: 〜だろう
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: the same meaning. 「だろう」 is the plain form, used mostly in men's speech and in writing; 「でしょう」 is polite and used by everyone.

similar.title: 〜かもしれない
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both express a guess. 「〜かもしれない」 means “maybe, possibly”, with low certainty (around 50%); 「〜でしょう」 shows the speaker thinks it is quite likely.

similar.title: 〜はずだ
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both express a guess, but 「〜はずだ」 rests on clear grounds or reasoning and is more certain: 「八時に出たから、もう着いているはずだ」.

similar.title: 〜のでしょうか
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「の」 is added before 「でしょうか」 to ask gently about a situation or reason: 「どうして遅れたのでしょうか」.

meaning: A plain-form guess: “probably ~”, “I suppose ~”. Also used to confirm something or to wonder to yourself. Common in men's speech and in writing.
connection: Plain form + だろう (no 「だ」 after na-adjectives and nouns)

senses.label: Guessing
senses.meaning: The plain form of 「でしょう」, showing the speaker's guess. Also common in news commentary and written texts.
senses.connection: Verb / i-adjective plain form / na-adjective stem / noun + だろう
examples: It will probably be sunny tomorrow.
He has probably gotten home by now.
This movie is sure to become popular.

senses.label: Confirming (rising tone)
senses.meaning: With rising intonation, it checks with or presses the listener: “~, right?”, “isn't it?”. Mostly men's speech, often shortened to 「だろ」. It sounds strong and can carry some blame.
senses.connection: Plain form + だろう？／だろ？
examples: See? It's just like I said, isn't it?
You're coming too, right?

senses.label: Wondering
senses.meaning: 「〜だろうか」 shows the speaker asking themselves or doubting: “I wonder ~”. 「〜のだろうか」 is also common.
senses.connection: Plain form + だろうか／のだろうか
examples: I wonder if it will snow tomorrow.
I wonder if he's really coming.

notes: Don't use 「だろう」 with elders, bosses or clients: 「部長も行くだろう？」 is very rude. Say 「部長もいらっしゃいますよね」 or use 「〜でしょうか」.
Don't add 「だ」 after nouns and na-adjectives: ✕「静かだだろう」 → ○「静かだろう」.
「〜だろ？」 with rising intonation sounds forceful, pushing “I'm right, aren't I?”. For the same meaning, women and polite situations mostly use 「〜でしょ？」.
「〜だろうか」 is wondering to yourself, “I wonder if ~”, not asking the other person. To ask someone, use 「〜でしょうか」.

etymology: 「だろう」 is a contraction of 「であろう」: the assertive 「で」 + 「あろう」 (the conjectural form of 「ある」). The final 「う」 comes from 「む」, an old auxiliary for guesses.
formation: 「だろう」 is a contraction of 「であろう」: the assertive 「で」 + 「あろう」 (the conjectural form of 「ある」). 「である」 asserts “it is ~”; adding the conjectural 「う」 gives “it will probably be ~”, softening the assertion into a guess. Contracted to 「だろう」 it becomes more conversational, and dropping the long vowel gives 「だろ」. With rising intonation the guess turns into checking with the listener, “~, right?”; adding 「か」 turns it into a question to yourself, “I wonder if ~”.

similar.title: 〜でしょう (guess / confirmation)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: the same meaning. 「でしょう」 is polite and used by everyone; 「だろう」 is plain, used mostly by men in speech but by everyone in writing.

similar.title: 〜だろうと思う
similar.explanation: Same origin: adding 「と思う」 after 「だろう」 presents the guess as your own opinion, which is softer and suits talking to others; 「だろう」 alone sounds more direct.

similar.title: 〜かもしれない
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both express a guess. 「〜かもしれない」 is less certain and only says it's possible; 「〜だろう」 shows the speaker thinks that is more or less the case.

similar.title: 〜のだろうか
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「の」 is added before 「だろうか」 to wonder about a reason or situation: 「彼はなぜ来なかったのだろうか」.

meaning: Presents the preceding content as “the situation” to explain it: giving a reason, asking for one, confirming or realizing new information; the casual 「〜んだ」 can also stress determination or give a command.
connection: Plain form + んです／のです (casual: んだ／のだ); nouns / na-adjectives: 〜なんです／なんだ; commands: dictionary form + んだ
etymology: It is made of the formal noun 「の」 + the copula 「だ」. 「の」 wraps up the sentence before it as “a matter”, and 「だ」 asserts “that's how it is”, which gives it an explaining, emphasizing tone. 「んだ」 is the spoken sound change of 「のだ」.
formation: Made of the formal noun 「の」 + the assertive auxiliary 「だ」. 「の」 packages the sentence before it as “a matter, a situation”, and 「だ」 asserts “that's how it is”. So 「〜のだ」 isn't a simple statement of fact but “presenting a situation as an explanation”: said to someone else, it explains a reason (actually, here's how it is); said to yourself, it's a realization (so that's how it is). Used with an action that hasn't happened yet (「行くんだ」), it asserts “going, that's how it is”, which produces a tone of determination or command. In speech, 「の」 weakens to 「ん」, giving 「んだ」 and 「んです」.

senses.label: Explaining a reason or situation
senses.meaning: The speaker explains their situation or reason: “It's that ~”, “The thing is ~”. Compared with plain 「〜です」, it adds an explaining tone.
senses.connection: Plain form + んです (nouns / na-adjectives: なんです)
examples: Sorry I'm late. The train stopped.
I have a headache today.
Actually, I'm getting married next month.

senses.label: Asking for the reason
senses.meaning: After noticing something, you ask for the reason or details, with a tone of concern or curiosity: “What happened?”, “Why ~?”.
senses.connection: Plain form + んですか／のですか
examples: What's wrong?
Why are you studying Japanese?
You look pale. Do you have a cold?

senses.label: Confirming new information
senses.meaning: 「〜んですね」 and 「〜なんですか」 confirm something you just learned: “Oh, so that's how it is.”
senses.connection: Plain form + んですね／なんですか
examples: Wow, so Tanaka-san is a good cook.
Tomorrow is a day off? I didn't know that.

senses.label: Realization
senses.meaning: The speaker suddenly understands a situation, like “Oh, so ...”. Often with 「そうか」 or 「なんだ」, in the plain 「〜んだ」.
senses.connection: そうか／なんだ + plain form + んだ
examples: Oh right, it's Sunday today, so it's closed.
Huh, so you already knew.

senses.label: Strong claim / determination
senses.meaning: States a claim or determination strongly, like “I will ...!” or “I'm telling you ...”. In writing, 「のだ／のである」 is used.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + んだ／のだ; often with 「絶対に」 or 「どうしても」
examples: I'm definitely going to become a doctor.
If you work hard, you can surely do it.

senses.label: Command / urging
senses.meaning: 「〜んだ」 can give a firm order or urge someone, usually from a superior to a junior or from a parent to a child, like “Go ...!”.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + んだ
examples: It's late, so go to bed now.
Stop crying and tell me properly.

notes: Don't add 「んです」 when simply stating a fact: 「私は学生なんです」 sounds like you're making an excuse or stressing special circumstances. In a self-introduction, 「学生です」 is enough.
「どうして〜んですか」 pressing someone about what they did sounds accusing: 「どうして来なかったんですか」 is very rude to a boss. You can ask 「何かあったんですか」 instead.
Nouns and na-adjectives need 「な」: ✕「学生んです」 → ○「学生なんです」.

「〜んですか」 presses for the reason behind something, so asking about someone's private life with it is rude: ✕「どうして結婚しないんですか」. The command use of 「〜んだ」 (「早く寝るんだ」) is very strong and is only for children or younger people.

similar.title: 〜んですが (preface)
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「が」 is added after 「〜んです」 to explain the situation first and then lead into a request or question: 「道に迷ったんですが、駅はどこですか」.

similar.title: 〜わけだ
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: it also has an explanatory “so that's why” tone, but 「〜わけだ」 focuses on reaching a natural conclusion from the facts: 「十年住んでいたから、日本語が上手なわけだ」.

similar.title: 〜のだから・〜んだから
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「〜のだ」 + 「から」. It presents a situation the listener also knows as the reason, often followed by a demand or judgment (「子どもなんだから、仕方ない」), and sounds stronger than 「から」.

meaning: Placed after a name it means “called ~ / named ~”, used to introduce or ask about names; 「NというN」 stresses “every single N”, and after a quantity word it stresses “as many as ~”; after a whole clause it states the content of nouns like 「考え」, 「話」 or 「気持ち」 (“the idea / news that …”).
connection: Noun (name) + という + noun; 何という + noun; noun + という + the same noun; 何十／何百／何千／何万 + という + noun; plain form / quotation 「…」 + という + noun (考え・話・気持ち, etc.)
etymology: 「という」 comes from the quoting particle 「と」 + 「言う」 and is used for definitions and names. 「NというN」 literally means “an N called N”, that is, “anything that can be called N”, which gives the meaning “all”. With numbers, it adds an exaggerated sense of “as many as ...”.
formation: 「という」 is made of the quoting 「と」 plus 「言う」 and originally means “called ...”. 「家という家」 literally is “the houses called ‘houses’”, i.e. “everything that deserves the name ‘house’”: using the name to enclose every member of the whole category, so it means “all ...”. After a quantity word such as 「何万」, 「という」 presents the number as a so-called figure, with a tone of surprise, “as many as that”. Both uses exploit the naming and quoting function of 「という」 to emphasize range or quantity.

senses.label: Introducing a name
senses.meaning: Tells the listener a name they may not know: “a ~ called …”.
senses.connection: Name + という + noun (人・店・町・本, etc.)
examples: There's a café called “Sakura” in front of the station.
You had a call from someone named Yamada.
This is a Japanese dish called “sushi”.

senses.label: Asking for a name
senses.meaning: 「何という〜」 asks for a name. In speech, people often say 「なんていう〜」.
senses.connection: 何という／なんという／なんていう + noun
examples: What is this flower called?
What's that singer's name again?

senses.label: Casual 「っていう」
senses.meaning: In casual conversation it often becomes 「〜っていう」, with the same meaning.
senses.connection: Name + っていう + noun
examples: A bakery called “Hana” opened in front of the station.

senses.label: Every single ...
senses.meaning: The same noun is repeated with 「という」 in between to mean “every ..., all ...”, with no exceptions. It is often followed by 「すべて」, 「みな」 or 「どこも」. Mostly used in writing and descriptions.
senses.connection: Noun + という + the same noun (common: 家という家・窓という窓・店という店・人という人)
examples: The typhoon damaged every single house in the village.
I opened every window to air out the room.
Every bone in my body hurts.

senses.label: As many as ...
senses.meaning: After number words like 「何百」, 「何千」, 「何万」 or 「数千」, it stresses a very large number: “hundreds of”, “tens of thousands of”. It sounds amazed.
senses.connection: 何十 / 何百 / 何千 / 何万 / 数万 etc. + という + noun
examples: Tens of thousands of people gathered at the venue.
I get hundreds of emails every day.

senses.label: Stating content
senses.meaning: 「という」 links a clause or a quotation to a noun such as 考え・意見・気持ち・不安・話・ニュース・意識・評価・ルール, and tells what that thought, news or feeling actually is: “the idea / news that …”. It does not mean “called” here — what comes before という is a whole sentence, not a name.
senses.connection: Plain form (nouns and な-adjectives may add 「だ」) / quotation 「…」 + という + noun (考え・話・気持ち・ニュース, etc.)
examples: I have this fear that I might fail, so I can't bring myself to try new things.
The idea that children are beings the whole of society should protect is spreading.
I heard the news that the bookstore in front of the station is closing next month.

notes: 「〜という人」 implies “someone I (or you) don't know”. Using 「という」 for someone the listener knows, or for a superior, sounds distant and disrespectful: ✕「田中部長という人が来ました」 → ○「田中部長がいらっしゃいました」.
Things everyone knows usually don't take 「という」: say 「東京に住んでいます」, not 「東京という町に住んでいます」, which sounds like introducing a place the listener has never heard of.
The colloquial 「っていう」 doesn't belong in formal situations or documents: ✕「ABCっていう会社から電話がありました」 → ○「ABCという会社から…」.
「NというN」 must repeat the same noun: ✕「家という建物」→ ○「家という家」.

Don't confuse it with the naming 「〜という」: 「田中という人」 is “a person called Tanaka”, not “all people”. In 「失敗するという不安」, on the other hand, a whole sentence comes before という and explains what the anxiety is (“the fear that I'll fail”), so don't translate it as “called” either.

similar.title: 〜と言う (quotation)
similar.explanation: Same origin: the same 「と」 + 「言う」, used as a full verb to quote what someone said: 「先生は明日休みだと言いました」. In this pattern 「という」 is followed by a noun and just gives it a name.

similar.title: 〜というのは
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「という」 + 「の」 + 「は」, used to define or explain a word: 「『KY』というのは、空気が読めないという意味です」.

similar.title: 〜ということ (nominalizer)
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「という」 + 「こと」 turns the content of a whole sentence into a noun; what comes before is a sentence, not a name: 「彼が結婚するということを聞いた」.

similar.title: 〜に至るまで
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both stress wide range with no exceptions. 「〜に至るまで」 names the far end of a range (「子どもから老人に至るまで」); 「NというN」 repeats the same noun to vividly mean “every single one”.

similar.title: 〜って (quotation, topic)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: in casual speech 「って」 can replace 「という」 or 「というのは」: 「『ハナ』って店、知ってる？」. Only used in conversation between people who know each other.
